strengths: The proposed loss-vector embedding idea is simple, intuitive, and potentially useful: assigning clients by the pattern of their losses across multiple models is a natural extension of IFCA and helps explain why lowest-loss assignment can fail under poor initialization.

The paper evaluates the method across several task types, including supervised image/text classification and unsupervised image reconstruction, and compares against a broad set of CFL/PFL baselines. The image-task results show strong and often fast cluster recovery, with CLoVE frequently reaching high ARI within a few rounds.

The method is practically attractive in settings where the number of clusters is known: it is easy to implement, uses generic losses rather than task-specific similarity metrics, and can apply to unsupervised objectives where many PFL baselines are less applicable.
The manuscript includes useful ablations on matching, clustering choice, and square-root losses, plus additional appendix experiments on harder label skews and mixed linear regression.
weaknesses: The theoretical support has serious gaps and apparent errors. For example, the appendix treats E[L] as E[F]^2 for F=sqrt(L), which is not generally true for a scaled chi random variable, and the concentration/union-bound argument for vector norms appears to miss dimension factors. These issues undermine the claimed one-shot recovery and exponential convergence guarantees.

The theory does not substantiate the broad claims made in the abstract. It is limited to mixed linear regression with Gaussian covariates, small noise, known K, well-separated unit-norm optima, balanced clusters, independently resampled client data each round, and either orthonormal or already proximal model collections. The practical algorithm uses ordinary loss vectors, while the strongest proof is for square-root loss vectors.

The privacy discussion is inadequate and overclaims: the manuscript states that loss vectors reveal nothing beyond cluster membership, but per-client losses across K server-chosen models can leak distributional or membership information, and no formal privacy analysis or mitigation is provided.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper lists baseline repositories and compute, but CLoVE/IFCA/FedAvg are self-implemented without a released link, and many important details are missing or underspecified, including exact architectures, preprocessing, client sampling, hyperparameter tuning fairness, and baseline adaptation details.

The experimental setup relies mostly on synthetic client partitions with known K and relatively small numbers of clients/seeds. Only three random seeds are used, and there is little discussion of sensitivity to K misspecification, unbalanced clusters, partial participation, noisy clients, or realistic FL constraints.

The significance claims are overstated. CLoVE is strong on many image skew settings, but it is not uniformly state of the art: FedAvg dominates Amazon Review accuracy, FlexCFL often achieves perfect ARI in image skews, and some improvements over IFCA are modest depending on the setting.

Communication and systems costs are underanalyzed. Each selected client receives all K models and evaluates all K losses every round, which can be expensive for large K or large models; the paper does not compare this overhead with baselines.

The manuscript does not provide a serious limitations or ethics section. Important limitations such as known cluster count, privacy leakage through loss vectors, scalability, and applicability beyond artificially constructed clusters are not sufficiently acknowledged.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in personalized/clustered federated learning: recovering unknown client clusters while training cluster-specific models under heterogeneous data. A method that works in both supervised and unsupervised settings would be useful if robustly established.

The core idea of clustering clients by their vector of losses across multiple candidate models is simple, intuitive, and easy to integrate with FedAvg-style training. The algorithm is clearly specified at a high level, including model-averaging and gradient-averaging variants.

The empirical section includes a reasonably broad set of baselines and tasks: image classification, text classification, and unsupervised reconstruction across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, Amazon Reviews, and AG News. The paper also reports ARI, not only downstream accuracy, which is appropriate for clustered FL.

The paper includes a theoretical analysis for mixed linear regression and attempts to connect loss-vector separation to cluster recovery, plus ablations on matching, clustering method, and square-root loss.
weaknesses: The central claims are substantially overclaimed relative to the evidence. The conclusion says CLoVE “substantially outperforms the state of the art,” but the reported tables contain several clear counterexamples: FedAvg is far better on Amazon Reviews accuracy, FlexCFL is better on AG News accuracy, IFCA is better on CIFAR-10 unsupervised reconstruction, and in additional label-skew settings CLoVE is sometimes below FedAvg, CFL, or local-only. This weakens both soundness and presentation.

The originality is modest. Loss-based assignment is already central to IFCA, and the main change is clustering full loss vectors plus bipartite matching. This is a plausible heuristic, but the paper does not convincingly distinguish it from natural extensions of IFCA or other embedding-based CFL methods, nor does it provide enough conceptual insight to justify the strong novelty language.

The theory is narrow and does not support the broad empirical claims. It applies to a highly stylized mixed linear regression model with Gaussian features, tiny noise, unit-norm and well-separated optima, small K, fresh independent samples each round, and either orthonormal or already proximal model collections. These assumptions are far from the neural-network, non-IID, finite-client settings emphasized in the paper.

Some theoretical statements are vague or hard to verify as written. Theorems rely on “suitably initialized” k-means, unspecified large constants, polylog factors, and asymptotic conditions such as dK^4 polylog(M)=o(nM). The connection from these conditions to the practical algorithm with K models and random neural initializations is not adequately justified.

The privacy discussion is not sound. The manuscript claims that sending loss vectors “does not reveal anything about the data,” which is false in general: per-client losses across multiple models can leak membership, label distribution, difficulty, outliers, or sensitive cluster attributes. Since the work is in federated learning, this is a material ethical and methodological concern.

The experimental design leaves important gaps. The method assumes the number of clusters K is known and mostly uses synthetic partitions with clean ground-truth clusters. There is little stress testing under misspecified K, imbalanced clusters, partial participation, client dropout, unequal data sizes, dynamic/streaming clients, or clusters that are not cleanly separable by loss vectors.

The evaluation uses only three random seeds and reports no statistical tests. Some gains are small relative to standard deviations, while strong claims are made from them. Runtime, communication, and memory costs are also underanalyzed, despite CLoVE requiring each selected client to evaluate all K models each round.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper links baseline repositories but lists CLoVE, IFCA, FedAvg, and local-only as self-implemented without providing a CLoVE code link. Model architecture descriptions are high-level, and details such as exact client splits, initialization procedures, hyperparameter tuning protocol, k-means initialization, and baseline adaptation choices are insufficient for reliable reproduction.

Presentation quality is uneven. The paper repeatedly makes broad claims not aligned with its own tables, contains duplicated/awkward phrasing, and has noisy or poorly rendered extracted figure/table text in the appendix. The limitations discussion is minimal and does not honestly engage with the method’s dependence on known K, loss-vector privacy leakage, initialization/clustering failure modes, or communication overhead.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and appealing clustered FL mechanism: represent each client by its vector of losses over K candidate models, cluster those embeddings, match clusters to models, and train cluster-specific models. This is an intuitive extension of IFCA that addresses a real failure mode of assigning each client only to its minimum-loss model.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this area, covering supervised image classification, text classification, and unsupervised reconstruction, with comparisons to FedAvg, local training, several PFL methods, and several CFL methods. CLoVE is consistently strong on the main image benchmarks, often achieving perfect ARI and competitive or best accuracy, and the initialization study directly supports the central robustness claim relative to IFCA.

The paper provides nontrivial theoretical support in a mixed linear regression setting, including one-shot recovery guarantees for square-root loss vectors under separation/concentration conditions and exponential convergence once accurate matching is maintained. The analysis helps explain why loss-vector clustering can be easier than clustering raw data or using only the argmin loss.

The method is practically attractive: it is easy to implement using standard clustering and bipartite matching, applies to supervised and unsupervised objectives as long as a loss is available, and does not require labels for the clustering step.
Presentation is generally clear, with useful figures, detailed appendix proofs, baseline code references, compute information, and ablations for matching, clustering choice, and square-root losses.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are much narrower than the empirical claims. They rely on mixed linear regression with Gaussian covariates/noise, small noise, known K, balanced per-cluster sample assumptions, orthonormal or already proximal model initialization, and suitably initialized k-means centers. This supports the intuition but does not fully justify the broad claims for deep nonconvex models and realistic FL deployments.

The paper overstates privacy. It claims that sending loss vectors to the server 'does not reveal anything about client data' beyond cluster information, but losses can leak membership, label distribution, outlier behavior, or other client attributes, especially across rounds and models. There is no formal privacy analysis, differential privacy, secure aggregation protocol, or empirical leakage study.

Reproducibility is only partial. Baseline repositories are listed, but CLoVE/IFCA/FedAvg are self-implemented without a released code link. Model architectures, tuning protocols, client sampling fractions, initialization details, and baseline hyperparameter fairness are not described at a level that would make exact reproduction straightforward. Only three random seeds are used.

The evaluation is strong but mostly synthetic in its federated heterogeneity: clients are constructed by label skew, feature rotation, or label permutation on standard datasets. The paper does not test naturally federated datasets, partial participation at scale, stragglers/dropout, communication cost, or the overhead of broadcasting/evaluating all K models at every round, which are important for practical FL significance.

Several results temper the strongest claims. On Amazon Reviews, FedAvg substantially outperforms CLoVE; on AG News, FlexCFL is better; and in some additional label-skew settings CLoVE is similar to or below IFCA/FlexCFL/FedAvg in accuracy. The paper acknowledges some of this but still uses broad language such as substantially outperforming the state of the art.

The method assumes the number of clusters K is known and fixed, while the conclusion only mentions dynamic splits/merges as future work. Sensitivity to misspecified K is not evaluated, despite K being central to both the algorithm and the claimed personalization setting.

There are some presentation and consistency issues. For example, the appendix explanation of scaling with number of clients says that more clients increase the dimension of the loss vector, but the loss-vector dimension is the number of models K, not the number of clients. Algorithm notation also appears to cluster over all M clients after sampling a subset. These do not invalidate the paper, but they reduce confidence in details.

The paper has no explicit limitations or ethics section. This is especially noticeable because the work is in federated learning and makes privacy-adjacent claims. The absence of a careful limitations discussion weakens the treatment of deployment risks, leakage, and fairness across client groups.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and intuitive clustered PFL method: represent each client by its vector of losses under multiple candidate models, cluster these embeddings, then train cluster-specific models. This directly targets a real weakness of IFCA-style assignment by argmin loss, and the motivating example is clear.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this area, covering supervised image classification, text classification, and unsupervised reconstruction, with several heterogeneity regimes including label skew, feature skew, concept shift, unknown K, early stopping, and partial participation.

The reported clustering results are strong: CLoVE frequently reaches ARI 1.0 within 2-3 rounds on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and FMNIST settings, and substantially improves over IFCA, CFL-S, FeSEM, PACFL, and FlexCFL in several challenging concept/feature shift cases.
The unsupervised applicability is a meaningful practical advantage over several PFL baselines, since the method only requires a model loss and does not require labels or class prototypes.

The paper includes nontrivial theoretical analysis for mixed linear regression, showing one-shot cluster recovery and fast convergence under separation/SNR assumptions, plus ablations on initialization, unknown number of clusters, and communication/computation overhead.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are much narrower than the empirical claims. They assume Gaussian mixed linear regression, known K, fresh i.i.d. samples per round, small noise/high SNR, balanced enough clusters, and either d orthonormal models or already proximal models. This does not closely match the neural-network experiments with K models and PyTorch random or identical initialization.

There is a notable mismatch between the main algorithm and parts of the theory: the proof of first-round recovery relies on N=d orthonormal square-root-loss vectors, while the practical algorithm generally uses K or K-hat models and ordinary losses. The paper notes this but does not fully bridge the gap, so the strongest theoretical statement only partially supports the implemented method.

Some claims of state-of-the-art performance are overstated. CLoVE is not consistently best in test accuracy: FedAvg is much better on Amazon Reviews and sometimes competitive or better when client distributions are similar; FlexCFL or CFL-S outperform CLoVE in some appendix settings. The paper explains some cases, but the headline wording remains too broad.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The baseline source links are listed, but the CLoVE/self-implemented code link appears blank in the manuscript, and several implementation details are underspecified, including exact model architectures, number of seeds, baseline tuning parity, clustering choices, early-stopping thresholds across experiments, and whether communication/computation budgets are strictly matched.

The comparison to baselines would be stronger with more careful fairness analysis. Some baselines may be disadvantaged by hyperparameters or by settings tailored to loss-vector separability; meanwhile CLoVE sends all models to clients during clustering and requires evaluating each local dataset on all candidate models, so wall-clock and communication measurements would be useful rather than mostly qualitative discussion.

The privacy discussion is honest but underdeveloped. Loss vectors can leak distributional information about clients, especially because they are explicitly used to infer client clusters; the paper does not provide privacy attacks, formal privacy guarantees, or experiments with differential privacy noise despite positioning the method for federated learning.

Presentation is generally clear, but the manuscript is long and occasionally difficult to audit because important caveats and additional results are pushed to appendices. The extracted PDF also suggests some figure/table rendering or font issues in the appendix, which could hinder readability.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and understandable clustered FL mechanism: represent each client by its losses under several candidate models, cluster those loss vectors, and use matching to associate clusters with models. The idea is practically attractive and easy to implement.

The manuscript contains a reasonably broad empirical suite across image classification, text classification, and autoencoder reconstruction, with comparisons to several CFL/PFL baselines. The initialization experiments and partial-participation appendices are useful stress tests.

The authors attempt to provide theory rather than only empirical evidence, and the linear-regression analysis gives some intuition for why loss vectors can separate clients even when raw data clusters overlap.
The method’s applicability to unsupervised reconstruction tasks is a genuine plus, since many personalized FL methods rely on labels or supervised objectives.
weaknesses: The central claims are much broader than the evidence supports. The theory is restricted to Gaussian mixed linear regression with unit-norm separated optima, small noise/high SNR, fresh iid samples each round, known K, and either d orthonormal initial models or already proximal models. This is far from the deep supervised/unsupervised FL settings used in the experiments.

There is a mismatch between the theoretical algorithm and the practical algorithm. The proof uses square-root loss vectors and special model collections, while the main algorithm and most experiments appear to cluster ordinary loss vectors with K models. The theorem also assumes suitably initialized k-means centers, which is a nontrivial condition for the claimed one-shot recovery.

The empirical evaluation relies heavily on synthetic partitions of standard centralized datasets, where ground-truth clusters are constructed from labels, rotations, or label permutations. This does not convincingly establish robustness in realistic federated populations with natural client heterogeneity. The FEMNIST unknown-cluster experiment is too limited and lacks strong comparative analysis.

The baseline comparison is not fully convincing. Several baselines are taken from different codebases or self-implemented, but tuning parity is unclear. Some reported baselines perform implausibly poorly in many settings, and the paper does not provide enough detail to rule out implementation or hyperparameter disadvantages.

Only three random seeds are used despite high variance in several results. The paper reports many near-perfect ARI numbers, but does not sufficiently analyze failure modes, sensitivity to K, client counts per cluster, unbalanced clusters, noisy labels, adversarial clients, or loss-scale/pathological calibration issues.

The claimed low communication and computation overhead is not adequately quantified. Before stability, every participating client evaluates and receives all models, which can be substantial for modern models. The paper argues this is small after early stopping, but provides no rigorous wall-clock, bandwidth, or memory comparison against baselines.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The text says the CLoVE code is publicly available, but the actual self-implemented code link appears missing/blank in the extracted manuscript. Model architectures and baseline tuning details are also too vague for reliable reproduction.

The privacy discussion is weak for an FL paper. CLoVE reveals per-client loss vectors across multiple models, and the authors explicitly state that the privacy implications are underexplored. There is no attack evaluation, DP implementation, or formal privacy guarantee.

Presentation is generally readable, but the paper repeatedly overstates conclusions, e.g. claims of optimal cluster recovery and state-of-the-art performance despite narrow assumptions and several tables where FedAvg or other baselines match or outperform CLoVE in accuracy. The limitations are not treated with enough seriousness.

strengths: The core idea is simple and appealing: represent each client by its vector of losses under multiple candidate models, cluster these loss vectors, and then use matched clusters to train personalized models. This is easy to understand, broadly applicable to supervised and unsupervised objectives, and avoids the brittle argmin assignment used by IFCA.

The empirical evaluation is extensive. The paper compares against many CFL and PFL baselines across image classification, text classification, and autoencoder reconstruction tasks, with several heterogeneity types including label skew, feature skew, concept shift, unknown K, partial participation, and client scaling. CLoVE often achieves perfect or near-perfect ARI within a few rounds and competitive or best test performance.

The paper provides useful ablations and diagnostics: initialization robustness against IFCA, matching ablations, alternative clustering methods, early stopping, and unknown-number-of-clusters experiments. These support the claim that loss-vector clustering is the decisive ingredient.

The theoretical analysis gives a plausible explanation for why loss-vector embeddings can separate clients even when raw data distributions overlap, and establishes high-probability recovery and exponential convergence in a mixed linear regression setting.

The discussion of overhead and privacy is relevant: the extra loss-vector communication is small relative to sending multiple model weights, early stopping reduces recurring overhead, and the paper correctly notes that aggregate loss sharing may have privacy implications requiring further study.
weaknesses: The theory is much narrower than the empirical claims. It assumes mixed linear regression with Gaussian features/noise, known fixed K, strong SNR/separation conditions, fresh iid data each round, and special orthonormal or proximal model configurations. This supports intuition but does not fully justify the broad claims about deep supervised and unsupervised FL settings.

Reproducibility is weaker than expected for a paper with this many baselines. The appendix lists baseline code sources, but the manuscript appears to leave the link for the authors' own CLoVE/self-implemented code blank. Hyperparameters are mostly described, but without released code and exact scripts, reproducing all baselines and partitioning protocols would be difficult.

Some empirical settings are synthetic and favorable to the method's assumptions. Many results rely on constructed clusters with known class/rotation/permutation structure and client train/test distributions matched exactly. More real-world federated datasets with naturally occurring latent clusters would strengthen the significance claim.

The method can be communication- and computation-heavy before stabilization because clients may need to evaluate all K models and the server may broadcast all models. The paper argues this is brief, but this depends on quick stabilization and small K; stress tests with larger K, larger models, and heterogeneous devices are limited.

The strongest accuracy gains are not universal. In several high-overlap label-skew cases, FedAvg or other baselines match or outperform CLoVE in test accuracy, and on text tasks the gains are modest or mixed. This is acknowledged, but it narrows the contribution to settings where cluster personalization is genuinely beneficial.

The privacy discussion is honest but incomplete. Sending per-client aggregate losses under multiple models may leak distributional or membership information, especially across rounds, and no formal privacy analysis or DP experiment is provided. This is not fatal, but it is material for federated learning.
